meta.reportLabel: Sterling back to +1: the one-in-eight economist poll that cut it was the ECB's, not the BoE's - markets price November 5 near 90% and Bailey says tolerance for energy inflation is running out.
meta.coverage: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, AUD, NZD, CAD, CHF · 28 pairs (full G10 ex SEK/NOK) + DXY + JPYBASKET + GER40 + EU50 + XAU + XAG + XCU + USOIL
meta.regime: Three scores move today and all three move because a source was traced back to its origin rather than quoted at second hand: the poll that cut sterling turns out to be the ECB's October survey, the Fed's own dot plot shows the policy rate held through 2027 rather than cut, and the RBNZ probability this report has been trading in both directions does not exist as a traded price at all. Underneath the corrections the board is almost perfectly flat - the entire G10 is inside 0.3% on the week against the dollar - because the week's whole distribution sits in one print on Wednesday.
meta.nextBigEvent: US September CPI on Wednesday October 14 at 12:30 UTC, where core at 0.2% m/m against a 0.20% Cleveland Fed nowcast is the only part the committee is deciding on; the 3.6-3.7% headline it will print measures September energy, and the Russian diesel waiver signed on October 9 lands entirely after that reference period.

dailyRead: Markets reopened at 05:00 UTC with the smallest weekly dispersion this report has recorded: DXY 102.209 is unchanged on the day and plus 0.04% on the week, USD/CHF and USD/CAD are both exactly flat on the week, and the widest weekly move in the G10 is USD/JPY at plus 0.29%. Nothing has moved, which makes this the right morning to fix three numbers rather than to chase a price, and the three corrections change scores in a way yesterday's report would not have predicted. The largest is sterling, and it is a reversal of this report's own call from twenty-four hours ago. GBP was cut from plus 1 to 0 on the claim that the November 5 hike was priced at 81% by the rates market while only about one in eight economists polled by Reuters expected it - described as the widest market-versus-forecaster gap on the board. That poll is not a Bank of England poll. The Reuters survey conducted October 5 to 8 found 70 of 73 economists expecting the ECB to hold on October 29 and 64 of 73 expecting a quarter-point ECB hike on December 17; it is a euro-area survey, and the article that carries the 81% LSEG figure for the BoE reports no economist poll for the BoE at all. So the gap that justified the cut did not exist. What does exist runs the other way. Money markets now price roughly 90% for a quarter-point move to 4.00% on November 5, up from 81%, with Oxford Economics citing the same 90% and expecting hikes in November and February; Berenberg expects one and doubts it starts a cycle, which is a disagreement about the path, not about the move. The September hold was 6-3 with Greene, Mann and Pill dissenting for 4.00% - Greene has now voted to hike at June, July and September - and Bailey hardened in public at the Istanbul Economic Forum on October 8, saying the Bank's tolerance for energy-driven inflation is running out, that a look-through approach only works if inflation expectations stay anchored to target, that the October 28 Budget must be credible and be seen as credible by markets, and that we cannot in any way be relaxed about the current state of financial markets. His energy argument got stronger over the weekend: UK gas printed 204.00 GBp/thm this morning, plus 11.12% on the week and plus 176.39% year to date, with EU storage about 12 percentage points below last year. Sterling goes back to plus 1 and EUR/GBP is the cleanest way to hold it. The second correction is the Fed, read from the September projection table on federalreserve.gov rather than from a summary. The median fed funds midpoint is 4.1% for 2026 and 4.1% again for 2027, falling to 3.9% only in 2028 - yesterday's file had 3.9% as the second year and therefore implied a 2027 cut the dots do not contain. The current midpoint is 3.875%, so the median is exactly one more quarter-point move and then a hold through all of next year, and the dispersion is tiny: of 18 participants, 12 sit on the 4.125% median, 4 above and 2 below. The September vote was unanimous 12-0, and the minutes released October 7 record all 19 officials supporting it, including the three who had dissented for a hike in July. A 12-0 vote with 12 of 18 dots on the median is the most consensual hawkish central bank on this board, and it is the floor under USD plus 2 even as December pricing drifts into a 65-75% range. The third correction closes a question this report has had open for four sessions. Centralbank.watch states plainly that New Zealand has no futures market tracking the Official Cash Rate directly, that the closest liquid contract settles on the 90-day bank bill, and that its odds are a guide to direction rather than a precise readout - and as of October 9 it publishes no probability for October 28 at all. So neither the 58% this report faded for three sessions nor the 88% it retreated to yesterday was ever a traded price. The one thing the curve does say is that 56.7bp of RBNZ tightening is priced by February 17, which is two hikes, against an RBA expected to hold at 4.60%. That compresses the 185bp carry the AUD/NZD long is paid for toward about 128bp by February, so the kiwi goes from minus 2 to minus 1 and AUD/NZD conviction comes down from MEDIUM to LOW-MED. The euro also rises, from minus 1 to 0, on the same Reuters poll that corrected sterling: 64 of 73 economists expect an ECB hike on December 17, OAT-Bund has compressed to 138.10bp from roughly 159bp two Fridays ago, EUR/USD is actually up on the day, and the French censure risk is now spread across an October 13-19 debate, an October 20 revenue vote, October 27 and November 17, with the ordinance route unavailable until December 17 at midnight. The cap on the euro is the bank channel, which is real: the Euro Stoxx Banks index is minus 8.43% on the month, entered a correction on October 8 and sits at its lowest since June, with Societe Generale, Credit Agricole and Deutsche Bank all more than 15% off recent highs on a decade-high French-German spread and sovereign debt at roughly 13% of bank assets. Away from the policy board, the weekend's real story is energy, and it broke the way almost nobody would guess. The Houthis struck Riyadh's King Khalid airport again on Sunday after a Saturday attack that Al Jazeera reports killed 12 and wounded 309 - the deadliest attack in the kingdom in over a decade, though a second Al Jazeera report gives three killed and 36 wounded across Riyadh and Abha, so the casualty figures conflict and that is stated rather than resolved - and the Houthis claim they were targeting Aramco facilities as well as the airport. Crude fell anyway: WTI 90.409 is minus 1.57% and Brent 103.377 is minus 1.28% this morning. Two things outran the escalation. Riyadh has restored pipeline flows to about 3.5 million barrels a day, with France sending soldiers, radars and defence systems to protect the Yanbu terminal; and on October 9 Trump announced a deal with Putin under which OFAC issued General License 135 authorising transactions in Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027. US diesel futures fell 4% on Friday and European diesel futures tumbled as much as 8.3%. The non-obvious consequence is for Wednesday. The headline CPI the market is braced for - 3.6% to 3.7% on roughly 5% energy and 9% gasoline - measures September, and the waiver that is now suppressing those same prices was signed in October. Wednesday's headline is a backward-looking read on an energy complex that executive action has since moved to reverse three weeks before the midterms, which is the strongest argument yet for ignoring it and trading core at 0.2%. It also splits the energy complex cleanly, and this is the trade of the week behind the CPI: refined products and crude are politically capped, while natural gas has no deal, no spare capacity and European storage 12 points below last year. Gas is up double digits on the week while crude is down. That is why sterling and the euro both improve on an energy argument at the same moment USOIL stays RANGE and the Canadian dollar stays at minus 2 - WTI at 90.409 is sitting exactly on the Bank of Canada's own baseline of oil falling toward 75 dollars by mid-2027 from about 90 in the second quarter, which removes the hawkish oil argument from the Canadian case entirely.

today.headline: Restored from 0 to +1. The one-in-eight economist poll that cut it yesterday was the Reuters ECB survey of October 5-8, not a BoE poll; money markets now price November 5 near 90%, up from 81%, and Bailey said on October 8 that the Bank's tolerance for energy-driven inflation is running out.
today.read: This is a reversal of yesterday's own call and the reason is a sourcing error worth naming precisely, because the cut rested entirely on it. Yesterday's report described an 81% market probability for November 5 sitting against a roughly 12% economist consensus and called it the widest market-versus-forecaster gap on the board. The poll behind that 12% is the Reuters survey conducted October 5 to 8, which found 70 of 73 economists expecting the ECB to hold on October 29 and 64 of 73 expecting a quarter-point ECB hike on December 17. It is a euro-area survey. The article that carries the 81% LSEG figure for the Bank of England reports no economist poll for the Bank of England at all, and no BoE poll showing a one-in-eight consensus exists in today's search. So the gap that justified the cut was an artefact of reading the ECB panel as a BoE panel. What the evidence actually shows is alignment and a hawkish drift. Money markets price roughly 90% for a move to 4.00% on November 5, up from the 81% quoted on October 9, and Oxford Economics cites the same 90% while expecting hikes in both November and February; Berenberg expects one hike and doubts it begins a cycle, which is a disagreement about the path rather than about the event. The committee leg is stronger than this report has had it too: the September hold was 6-3 with Greene, Mann and Pill dissenting for 4.00%, and Greene has now voted to hike at three consecutive meetings. Bailey himself hardened on the record at the Istanbul Economic Forum on October 8, saying tolerance for energy-driven inflation is running out, that a look-through approach only works if inflation expectations stay anchored to target, that the October 28 Budget must be credible and be seen as credible by markets, and that we cannot in any way be relaxed about the current state of financial markets. His energy argument then got stronger over the weekend: UK gas printed 204.00 GBp/thm this morning, plus 0.71% on the day, plus 11.12% on the week and plus 176.39% year to date, with EU storage about 12 percentage points below last year and warnings it could end the winter below 30%. The fiscal counterweight is unchanged and is why this is plus 1 and not plus 2: the Bank has paused gilt sales for six months and stopped sales of 20- and 30-year gilts entirely, the 30-year went through 6% around October 1 for the first time since early 1998, the Budget lands a week before the decision, and Thursday's August GDP is forecast at minus 0.1% m/m after plus 0.4%. The ten-year is 5.4121% on TE this morning, down about 1bp from Friday, still the highest major yield in the world at 17.51bp over the Treasury and 192.61bp over the Bund. Sterling itself has done nothing - 1.32415, plus 0.03% on the day and plus 0.15% on the week - with 1.3140 the 2026 low holding support and 1.3274 then the September 30 peak at 1.3311 the levels to clear. Bailey speaks four times between Tuesday and Saturday, the October 16 appearance at 02:00 UTC a red folder, and September CPI on October 21 is the decider.

today.headline: Raised from -1 to 0 on the same Reuters poll that corrected sterling: 64 of 73 economists expect a December 17 ECB hike, OAT-Bund has compressed to 138.10bp, and the French censure risk is now spread across four dates rather than concentrated on one.
today.read: The euro has been scored on two constraints and both have loosened, while the hawkish forward has been documented properly for the first time. The Reuters survey of October 5 to 8 is the hardest forward number on this board: 70 of 73 economists expect the October 29 hold and 64 of 73 expect a quarter-point hike on December 17, when new projections arrive. ECB Watch prices the October hold at 88% with 12% on 2.75%. That is 88% of a 73-strong panel expecting the deposit rate to go to 2.75% in December, in the currency that is the worst major year to date at minus 4.55%, and a currency whose central bank is that widely expected to tighten cannot carry a minus 1. TE re-verified the deposit facility at 2.50%, in force since September 16, against a main refinancing rate of 2.65%, with September HICP at 3.8% from 3.2% and core at 2.5% pointing the same way. Lagarde has kept to meeting-by-meeting and said the Council had not discussed future steps; she speaks twice on Tuesday and Wednesday, at 02:10 and 08:30 UTC. On the sovereign leg the improvement has continued: OAT-Bund is 138.10bp this morning with the OAT at 4.8670% and the Bund at 3.4860%, against above 150bp on October 2 and roughly 159bp the Friday before that, which was the widest since November 2011. On the political leg the structure matters more than the headlines. The Assembly debates the first part of the budget in open session from October 13 to 19, votes the revenue half on October 20, the social security bill on October 27 and the whole text on November 17, and lawmakers have 70 days to debate and amend, with the ordinance route unavailable until that period expires on December 17 at midnight. Lecornu brings roughly 54bn euros of consolidation and a 5%-of-GDP deficit target to an Assembly where he has no majority; the left has promised censure and LFI and the left reached 260 of the 289 needed in February, while analysis suggests the RN may hesitate to topple a government and leave 2027 without a budget. None of that is a Tuesday event. What holds the euro at 0 rather than higher is the bank channel, and it is firing hard. The Euro Stoxx Banks index is minus 8.43% on the month on TE, entered a technical correction on October 8 and sits at its lowest since June, with Societe Generale, Credit Agricole and Deutsche Bank all more than 15% below recent highs. The drivers are the decade-high French-German spread, sovereign debt at roughly 13% of bank assets at end-2025, and crowding after a three-year rally that tripled the sector since 2022; Bloomberg's read is a reset rather than a crash, and one strategist expects pressure until yield curves and risk premia move sustainably lower. The price is already turning: EUR/USD is 1.12061, plus 0.05% on the day and only minus 0.15% on the week against minus 0.53% a week ago, though still minus 2.97% on the month. EUR/GBP at 0.84626 is the cross to watch, minus 0.30% on the week and minus 2.98% year to date, because it is where the euro upgrade meets the larger sterling upgrade and loses. Back to -1 if the bank correction extends or a motion carries after October 20; to +1 only if banks recover rather than merely bounce and December survives Lagarde's two appearances.

today.headline: Raised from -2 to -1. The October 28 probability this report traded in both directions does not exist - New Zealand has no OCR futures market - and the one thing the curve does price is 56.7bp of RBNZ tightening by February 17, which is two hikes.
today.read: This closes a question that has been open for four sessions and it closes against the position. For three sessions this report was short the kiwi on a market priced at 58% for an October hike against a Bank pointing to an October pause then December, with the repricing of that 58% as the payoff. Yesterday it retreated to 88% for no change from a tracker it flagged as stale. Centralbank.watch, the tracker in question, states the problem plainly: New Zealand has no futures market that tracks the Official Cash Rate directly, the closest liquid contract settles on the 90-day bank bill rate, and its odds are therefore a guide to direction rather than a precise readout. As of October 9 it publishes no probability for October 28 at all. So neither number was ever a traded price, and the correct action is to stop quoting a probability for this meeting rather than to pick between two that cannot be verified. The one row the page does carry is informative and it cuts the other way: February 17, 2027 at 100% higher, plus 56.7bp, taking the OCR to 3.32%. That is two hikes priced into the kiwi curve by February against an RBA widely expected to hold at 4.60%, and it compresses the carry differential this report has leaned on from 185bp toward roughly 128bp. A currency whose curve prices two hikes in four months is not a minus 2. The backward case is why it is still negative rather than neutral: Q2 CPI ran 4.1% against a 1-3% target with core at 3.2%, growth slowed to plus 0.2% q/q from plus 0.9%, unemployment rose to 5.6% from 5.4%, and this is still the weakest data set in the G10 relative to its policy rate. But the price has stopped confirming it - NZD/USD is 0.56054, minus 0.12% on the day but plus 0.11% on the week, with the ten-year at 5.0340% and down about 3.6bp from Friday. TE's forecast rows still carry 2.75% for October 28 and 3.00% for December 9, in line with the Bank's own September track, so the Bank and the curve now broadly agree and there is no gap left to trade. The direct consequence is on the best trade this report has carried: AUD/NZD stays LONG on level carry and on the RBNZ deciding six days before the RBA, but its conviction comes down from MEDIUM to LOW-MED, because the forward differential is narrowing rather than widening. Q3 CPI on October 21 is the only thing that can force October and an acceleration from 4.1% is what turns this hawkish; the Governor speaks October 15 and the general election is November 7.

today.headline: Held at +2, with the Fed's own projections read from source and more hawkish than this report has carried them: the median midpoint is 4.1% for 2026 and 4.1% again for 2027, with the first cut only in 2028, and 12 of 18 participants sit exactly on that median.
today.read: The dollar score does not change but its foundation does, and in the direction that makes it more durable. The September projection table on federalreserve.gov gives median fed funds midpoints of 4.1% for 2026, 4.1% for 2027, 3.9% for 2028, 3.6% for 2029 and 3.2% in the longer run. Yesterday's file carried 4.1% for the first year and 3.9% for the second, which implied a cut in 2027 that the dots do not contain - 3.9% is the 2028 median. Against a current midpoint of 3.875%, the median path is exactly one more quarter-point hike and then a hold through all of next year. The dispersion is the part worth trading: of 18 participants, 12 project the 4.125% median, 4 project 4.375% and only 2 project 3.875%, so 16 of 18 are at or above one more hike and two thirds of the committee is on a single dot. The same table carries PCE inflation at 3.7% for 2026 with core PCE at 3.4%, GDP growth at 2.3% and unemployment flat at 4.1% every year through 2029. The procedural record is just as tight: September was a unanimous 12-0 vote and the minutes released October 7 record all 19 officials supporting it, including Hammack, Kashkari and Logan, who had dissented for a hike in July. A 12-0 vote with two thirds of the dots on the median is the most consensual hawkish central bank on this board, and that is why December pricing drifting matters less than it looks. The drift is real - Defirate carries December 9 at roughly 65%, down from 71% a week earlier, against FedWatch above 75% and Kalshi at 65% on October 2 - but the committee's own distribution has not moved and October is priced at a hold with 20-25% on a hike. The supporting data remains the tension: September payrolls 29K, unemployment 4.2%, August CPI 3.4% with core 2.4%, annual growth 2.2%, and a ten-year at 5.2370% after a 22bn-dollar 30-year auction cleared near 5.618% with indirect bidders taking 72.3%, above the recent average, pulling the long end back from a 5.732% intraday high that was the highest since 2002. The price has gone nowhere: DXY 102.209, exactly unchanged on the day, plus 0.04% on the week, plus 2.84% on the month and plus 3.95% year to date. Wednesday is the single test and the shape is now clearer than ever. The calendar carries CPI y/y at 3.6% from 3.4%, m/m at 0.6% from 0.4%, core m/m at 0.2% from 0.3% and core y/y at 2.5% from 2.4%, with consensus and the Cleveland Fed nowcast both near 0.20% core and Polymarket putting 0.2% at 47.5%, 0.3% at 33.5%, 0.1% at 13.5% and 0.4% at 5.2%. The headline acceleration is energy and it is backward-looking in a way that is newly obvious: the Russian diesel waiver signed on October 9 lands entirely after September's reference period, so Wednesday measures prices that executive action has since moved to suppress. Core at 0.3% or above revives October; 0.2% or below leaves December as the only live date and takes this score to +1. Chairman Warsh speaks as a red folder on Friday at 03:30 UTC and has said inflation is too high and has been for too long.

today.headline: Held at -2 and the short is cleaner than yesterday allowed: WTI at 90.409 is minus 1.57% with a Saudi airport in ruins, and 90 dollars is exactly where the Bank of Canada's own baseline assumed crude would be on its way to 75 by mid-2027.
today.read: Yesterday's report added two unpriced bullish oil facts - a hurricane shutting in more than 60% of Gulf of Mexico crude capacity and an SPR near a record low - as a reason to size the Canadian short smaller. This morning tests that directly and it fails. The Houthis struck Riyadh's King Khalid airport again on Sunday after a Saturday attack that Al Jazeera reports killed 12 and wounded 309, the deadliest in the kingdom in over a decade, and claimed Aramco facilities were targeted too. Crude fell on it: WTI is 90.409, minus 1.57% on the day and minus 10.83% on the month, and Brent is 103.377 at minus 1.28%. Two supply responses outran the escalation. Riyadh has restored pipeline flows to about 3.5 million barrels a day, with France sending soldiers, radars and defence systems to protect the Yanbu terminal, and OFAC issued General License 135 on October 9 authorising Russian-origin diesel transactions through April 7, 2027, which took US diesel futures down 4% on Friday and European diesel futures down as much as 8.3%. A market that stops paying for a mass-casualty strike on the largest Gulf producer is a market pricing the risk premium out, not in. That removes the hawkish oil argument from the Canadian case entirely, and the Bank's own numbers show why it matters: Macklem told an audience in Halifax on September 21 that the Bank can look past a temporary gasoline jump but not persistent higher energy costs, and that oil near 100 dollars would push inflation up in the coming months - while the Bank's baseline assumed crude falling toward about 75 dollars by mid-2027 from roughly 90 in the second quarter of 2026. WTI at 90.409 is sitting on that baseline, not above it. The data case is unchanged and is the reason the verdict stays WEAKENING: employment fell 68.3K against a plus 6.1K forecast after August's minus 41.7K, 110K of jobs gone in two months, with unemployment up only 0.1pt to 6.5% because participation fell to 64.8%, the lowest since December 1997 outside 2020. The forward stays a dovish-leaning hold rather than a cut path: no cut is priced for October 28, roughly 27% hike odds survived the 74K miss, TD expects a hold through 2026 while markets carry at least one hike before year-end, and TD read the print as cooling hike talk rather than building a cut case. The Bank also sees Q4 growth roughly halved to below 1% if US tariffs stay in place. The one restraint on conviction is the price itself: USD/CAD is 1.42602, plus 0.02% on the day and exactly flat on the week for a second consecutive week, so the pair has twice absorbed bad Canadian news without a weekly gain, and the ten-year at 3.8780% is among the lowest major yields. Macklem speaks Wednesday at 06:05 UTC and Friday at 04:15 UTC; September CPI and the Survey of Consumer Expectations land October 19 and decide whether December gets priced, with 3.0% headline the thing that stops the Bank moving this month whatever the labour data says.

today.headline: Held at 0, with the October probability stated by instrument instead of picked: prediction markets price a hold at 91-95%, futures-derived estimates put the hike at 17-26%, and no source puts October above 26% - so the meeting is a hold with a tail.
today.read: Yesterday's report corrected 6% to 25-26% and announced the under-priced gap was gone. Today the honest version is that both numbers are real and they measure different instruments, which is a more useful thing to know than either figure. Kalshi carries 91% for maintaining the rate against 6% for a 25bp hike, and Polymarket's October 12 snapshot has no change at 95.3% against 4.1% - those are the prediction markets this report originally quoted at 6%. FXStreet reports futures giving the October hike 26%, and centralbank.watch has no change at 83%, implying 17% - those are the rate-market reads this report quoted yesterday. The actionable statement is the intersection: no source puts October 30 above 26%, so the meeting is priced as a hold with a meaningful tail, and TE's own forecast row for October 30 is 1.25%. Former executive director Kazuo Momma's 20-30% for consecutive hikes sits above the prediction markets and inside the futures range, so he is a modest hawk rather than a radical one, and he adds that a delay past January is extremely unlikely. Ueda said on October 6 that the Bank intends to continue raising the policy rate and adjusting the degree of accommodation in response to developments in activity, prices and financial conditions, which Bloomberg read as doing little to challenge the bets against a back-to-back move. Futures carry most of one hike by December and 2.02% by September 2027. The bond market continues to do the hawkish work: the ten-year JGB is 3.0160% after the October 6 auction cleared at 3.101% near a three-decade high, and the structural story behind that rally is intact - Takaichi telling parliament that Japan no longer needs reflationary policy built on monetary easing and fiscal expansion is a supply argument, less issuance, which is why the curve rallied on hawkish news rather than selling off. The yen itself continues to lose ground quietly: USD/JPY 158.358 is plus 0.03% on the day, plus 0.29% on the week - the widest weekly move in the G10 - and plus 2.60% on the month, on a Treasury-JGB gap still worth 222.10bp. The crosses tell the same story, with GBP/JPY plus 0.43% on the week the biggest weekly gainer as sterling was restored. For a 4H book the conclusion holds from yesterday and is now better grounded: the October 30 Outlook Report and its inflation forecast revision is the whole tradeable event, carry pays into it, and yen shorts should be sized for a meeting priced as a hold with a 1-in-4 tail rather than for a surprise in either direction. Invalidated if that report drops the overshoot language or if core CPI, at 1.7% and falling, keeps undershooting.

today.headline: Held at 0, with the cross that carried the signal now turning: EUR/CHF is 0.93071 and back above the 0.93 area Rabobank expects, after three consecutive weekly declines, while USD/CHF is exactly flat on the week at 0.83053.
today.read: The score is unchanged but the trade behind it flips, and the reason is the euro rather than the franc. Everything in the SNB's reaction function still argues for a weaker franc: the policy rate is 0%, the lowest in the G10, held for a fifth consecutive assessment on September 24 with the sight-deposit discount unchanged; the September statement dropped the specific bias against rapid franc appreciation; and on October 8 Vice Chairman Martin hinted at lower-for-longer while officials pushed back on near-term tightening. What this report has been trading against that is the euro cross, on the argument that a French binary event would force haven buying into the franc. Two things have changed. EUR/CHF has turned up - 0.93071, plus 0.08% on the day and minus 0.15% on the week, which snaps three consecutive weekly declines and puts it back above the 0.93 level Rabobank expects to hold. And the French event behind the bid is now dated properly: the Assembly's first solemn vote is October 20, the social security bill October 27, the whole text November 17, and the ordinance route is unavailable until December 17 at midnight, so there is no binary inside this week or next. With the euro upgraded to 0 on a December ECB hike that 64 of 73 economists expect, EUR/CHF goes from SHORT to RANGE. Against the dollar nothing has happened at all: USD/CHF at 0.83053 is plus 0.05% on the day and exactly 0.00% on the week, though plus 1.60% on the month and plus 4.75% year to date, so the dollar continues to beat the franc over every window longer than a week. Domestically there is no urgency and no story: September CPI at 1.0% from 0.8% with core at 0.5% sits comfortably inside the 0-2% band, unemployment is 3.0%, growth is 2.3% y/y and the ten-year is 0.5580%. The ceiling on any franc rally is still the SNB itself - Rabobank warns that an accelerated bout of franc buying this autumn could force intervention, and BNP Paribas carries 0.94 at three months and 0.92 at twelve, bracketing spot - and the bar for that intervention is a disorderly move rather than a directional one. Chairman Schlegel speaks Thursday at 04:30 UTC, the policy minutes land October 22 and the next assessment is December 10. Turns hawkish only if inflation keeps climbing off 1.0% while a haven bid persists; the franc crosses are otherwise a function of the European calendar, which has just moved a week further out.

today.headline: Quiet and unchanged at +1, with one figure corrected: TE now carries copper at 6.6866 USD/lb, plus 17.68% year to date and plus 30.87% over twelve months, not the plus 38.87% yesterday's file quoted, against iron ore minus 8.11% on the month.
today.read: The Australian case was untouched by the weekend and stays the second-best on the board, but the copper number this report has been quoting needs fixing and it matters because copper is the leg carrying the currency. TE this morning has copper at 6.6866 USD/lb, plus 0.66% on the day, plus 1.54% on the week, plus 5.63% on the month, plus 17.68% year to date and plus 30.87% over twelve months. Yesterday's file quoted plus 38.87% on the year; TE wins and the figure comes down. It is still the strongest physical commodity on this board by a distance, with refined-copper tariffs unresolved as a live upside risk, and the monthly gain has in fact accelerated. The cap is the other half of the terms of trade and it is the larger export: iron ore at 90.68 USD/T is minus 0.73% on the week, minus 8.11% on the month and minus 15.36% year to date, and that split is the whole reason this is plus 1 rather than plus 2. The policy supports are unchanged: a 4.60% cash rate after the unanimous September 29 hike, the highest in the G10 and the highest Australian rate since 2011, with August headline CPI at 4.0% but softer than economists expected and the trimmed mean the Bank actually weighs flat at 3.6% for a third month. Bullock signalled less follow-up tightening than futures carried, and November 3 is a hold as the base case with no published TE forecast and no precise probability re-verified today, so none is quoted. The currency has quietly become the best performer against the dollar in 2026: AUD/USD at 0.69770 is minus 0.09% on the day and plus 0.08% on the week, minus 2.28% on the month but plus 4.56% year to date and plus 7.10% over twelve months - the only major with a positive year-to-date figure against the dollar, which is worth holding in mind on a board where every other currency is negative. The week is dense and front-loaded: the September minutes on Tuesday, China September CPI on Wednesday where a miss hits both the currency and copper together, then September employment as a red folder at 00:30 UTC on Thursday, forecast at plus 20.0K after plus 39.5K with unemployment held at 4.6%. Q3 CPI on October 28 is what decides November and the trimmed mean is the number. Turns hawkish if that trimmed mean breaks above 3.6% after three flat months; down to 0 if Thursday's employment misses and copper gives back the week.

GBP.when: November 5 with a Monetary Policy Report, priced near 90% in money markets - up from 81% - with December 17 the following meeting.
GBP.note: Held at 3.75% on September 17 on a 6-3 vote, with Greene, Mann and Pill dissenting for 4.00%; Greene has now voted to hike at June, July and September. JPY.when: October 30 is priced as a hold - prediction markets at 91-95% no change, futures-derived estimates at 17-26% for a hike - with December the market's date for the move.

NZD.when: October 28, with no traded probability available - New Zealand has no OCR futures market - against 56.7bp of tightening priced by February 17.
NZD.note: Hiked to 2.75% on September 2, the third move of a cycle that ran 2.25% to 2.50% in July and then to 2.75%. The probability question this report has had open for four sessions is now closed, and against its own position. Q3 CPI on October 21 is the only thing that can force October; Q2 ran 4.1% against a 1-3% target with core at 3.2%, growth slowed to plus 0.2% q/q and unemployment rose to 5.6%. The Governor speaks October 15 and a general election follows November 7.

CAD.note: Held at 2.25% on September 2 for a seventh consecutive decision. The dovish-leaning hold stands and today the oil leg stops arguing against it. If US tariffs stay in place the Bank sees Q4 growth roughly halved to below 1%.

catalysts.note: Scheduled this week on previews ahead of the October 27-28 meeting, with no verified release time in today's calendar pull so none is quoted. Relevant only as a read on whether the labour softening visible in a 29K September payroll print is showing up in district reporting; the committee's own distribution has 12 of 18 dots on one number and will not move on it.

catalysts.event: Australia: September employment change and unemployment rate
catalysts.note: Forecast at plus 20.0K after plus 39.5K with unemployment held at 4.6% on the ForexFactory calendar. The input that shapes November 3 ahead of Q3 CPI on October 28, and the near-term test of the only major with a positive year against the dollar at plus 4.56%. A miss takes AUD toward 0 and hits AUD/JPY, AUD/CAD and AUD/NZD together, since all three are long the Australian leg - and it lands thirty hours before Bailey's red folder, which is why GBP/AUD is scored RANGE rather than held on either side.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB Chairman Schlegel speaks
catalysts.note: A week after Vice Chairman Martin hinted at lower-for-longer and officials pushed back on near-term tightening. The September assessment held at 0% for a fifth time, nudged CPI projections up and dropped the specific bias against rapid franc appreciation. EUR/CHF at 0.93071 is back above the 0.93 area Rabobank expects after three consecutive weekly declines, and Rabobank's warning that an accelerated bout of franc buying this autumn could force intervention is the thing to listen for. The policy minutes follow on October 22.

catalysts.event: UK: August GDP m/m
catalysts.note: Forecast at minus 0.1% m/m after plus 0.4% on the ForexFactory calendar - the clearest counterweight to a November hike now priced near 90%. A contraction the week the Bank's own governor says tolerance for energy inflation is running out is the tension in the sterling case, and it is why GBP is +1 rather than +2. Annual growth was revised to 1.4% y/y, so a negative month does not break the trend on its own; a materially worse print than minus 0.1% is what would reopen the question of whether the Bank hikes into a slowing economy a week after the Budget.

catalysts.event: UK: BoE Governor Bailey speaks
catalysts.note: Ninety minutes after August GDP, which makes this the most informative of his four appearances short of Friday's red folder: it is the first chance to hear how the Bank reads a negative growth month against the energy argument. Markets price November 5 near 90% and the Budget lands October 28, a week before the decision, on which he has already said fiscal policy must be credible and be seen as credible by markets.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ Governor speaks
catalysts.note: The only scheduled central-bank communication before October 28, and it carries more weight than usual because there is no traded probability for that meeting - New Zealand has no futures market tracking the OCR, so the curve's only published row is February 17 at plus 56.7bp to 3.32%. Anything that moves the October pause then December track the Bank set out in September has nothing to be measured against, which makes the words themselves the price. Q3 CPI on October 21 follows.

catalysts.event: US: September PPI and retail sales (plus jobless claims and the Philly Fed index)
catalysts.note: Four red folders at one time, thirty hours after CPI: PPI m/m forecast at 0.5% from 0.4%, core PPI at 0.3% from 0.2%, retail sales at 0.3% from 1.2% and core retail sales at 0.5% from 1.4%. The retail sales forecasts are the ones to watch, because both imply a sharp deceleration from August and would be the first hard sign that a 29K payroll print is reaching the consumer. Jobless claims at 195K from 197K and the Philly Fed at 26.5 from 37.8 are medium-impact on the same release. If CPI has already settled the core question, this is where the growth half of the dollar case gets tested.

catalysts.event: UK: BoE Governor Bailey speaks
catalysts.note: The red folder of the sterling week and the last scheduled chance to hear the Governor before September CPI on October 21. Markets price November 5 near 90%, the committee split 6-3 in September with Greene, Mann and Pill wanting 4.00%, and Bailey has already said the Bank's tolerance for energy-driven inflation is running out and that a look-through approach only works if inflation expectations stay anchored to target. With UK gas plus 11.12% on the week to a new high, an endorsement here takes GBP toward +2 and GBP/JPY, GBP/CAD and GBP/NZD with it.

catalysts.event: US: Fed Chairman Warsh speaks
catalysts.note: The Chair's first scheduled appearance after CPI, PPI and retail sales, and the voice behind the most consensual hawkish central bank on this board: September was a unanimous 12-0 vote, the October 7 minutes record all 19 officials supporting it including the three July hike dissenters, and 12 of 18 participants project the same 4.125% median for end-2026. He has said inflation is too high and has been for too long. Whatever CPI does to December pricing, now 65-75% across curves, this is where it gets confirmed or walked back.

catalysts.event: Canada: BoC Governor Macklem speaks
catalysts.note: His second appearance of the week, three days before September CPI and the Survey of Consumer Expectations. The question is unchanged and now sharper: with WTI at 90.409 sitting exactly on the Bank's own baseline path toward 75 dollars by mid-2027, the oil caveat that has kept roughly 27% hike odds alive after a 74K employment miss has lost its premise. Dropping it is what starts pricing December.

catalysts.event: UK: BoE Governor Bailey speaks
catalysts.note: The fourth and last appearance of the week, on a Saturday, so the market reaction lands at Monday's open rather than live. Useful mainly as a check on whether the message held across four outings in four days with a negative GDP print in the middle of them.

catalysts.event: Canada: September CPI and the BoC Survey of Consumer Expectations
catalysts.note: The release that decides whether December gets priced. August held at 3.0% headline with core at 2.4%, and 3.0% is the number that stops the Bank cutting this month whatever the labour data says. The Survey of Consumer Expectations is the part that matters more than usual, because Macklem's whole energy argument rests on whether a fuel shock is becoming persistent in expectations - and crude has now fallen back onto the Bank's own baseline.

catalysts.event: France: Assembly solemn vote on the 2027 budget's revenue half
catalysts.note: The first solemn vote and the nearest thing to a binary in the French sequence, a week later than this report had it before the timetable was checked. A censure motion can be filed at any point in the October 13-19 debate, but this is the first scheduled test. OAT-Bund at 138.10bp has already compressed 20bp from its widest since November 2011, so the market is pricing survival; the euro-area bank index, minus 8.43% on the month, is where a failure would show first.

catalysts.event: UK: September CPI
catalysts.note: The decider for November 5, two weeks before the meeting. August ran 3.1% headline with core at 2.6% and wage growth has decelerated to 3.9% from 4.2%, which is the disinflationary half of the argument. Against it: UK gas at plus 176.39% year to date, the consumer price cap up 9% in October, and a governor who says the Bank's tolerance for energy-driven inflation is running out. A print above consensus with pricing already near 90% takes GBP to +2.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Q3 CPI
catalysts.note: The only thing that can force October 28, one week out. Q2 ran 4.1% against a 1-3% target with core at 3.2%. With no traded OCR probability to reprice and 56.7bp already in the curve by February, this print is where the kiwi score gets decided rather than where a market gets corrected: an acceleration from 4.1% turns NZD hawkish and breaks the AUD/NZD long, a clear undershoot takes it back to -2.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB monetary policy meeting minutes
catalysts.note: The record of the September 24 assessment that held at 0% for a fifth time, nudged CPI projections up and dropped the specific bias against rapid franc appreciation. The question is how deliberate that drop was, since it is the single most dovish signal the SNB has sent this year and the reason the franc crosses are scored on European events rather than Swiss policy.

catalysts.event: France: Assembly solemn vote on the 2027 social security financing bill
catalysts.note: The second of three scheduled votes, a week after the revenue half and three weeks before the whole text on November 17. The ordinance route remains unavailable until the 70-day period expires on December 17 at midnight, which is why this sequence is a series of tests rather than a cliff.

catalysts.event: UK: Budget
catalysts.note: A week before the Bank of England decision, and Bailey has already put the Chancellor on notice that fiscal policy must be credible and be seen as credible by markets. Headroom has been cut to roughly 13.8bn pounds from 26bn on one estimate and about 12bn from 23.6bn on another, the 30-year went through 6% around October 1 for the first time since early 1998, and the Bank has paused gilt sales for six months while stopping 20- and 30-year sales entirely. The house view in sterling research is that the currency stays capped into this event and recovers after it if the Budget passes as a non-event; a fiscal premium that widens further is what takes GBP back to 0.

catalysts.event: Australia: Q3 CPI
catalysts.note: Six days before the November 3 decision and the number that actually decides it. The trimmed mean the RBA weighs has held at 3.6% for three months while headline rose to 4.0% and printed softer than economists expected. A break above 3.6% turns AUD hawkish; a clear undershoot with Thursday's employment also missing takes it to 0.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ Official Cash Rate decision
catalysts.note: A hold is the base case on the Bank's own September track and on TE's forecast rows, which carry 2.75% here and 3.00% for December 9. No probability is quoted because none is traded: New Zealand has no futures market tracking the OCR and the nearest liquid contract settles on the 90-day bank bill. The decision lands six days before the RBA, which is the remaining edge in the AUD/NZD long now that the repricing case has gone.

catalysts.event: Canada: Bank of Canada decision and Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.note: A seventh hold is the base case with no cut priced and roughly 27% hike odds surviving a 74K employment miss. The Monetary Policy Report is the part to read, because its oil assumption is now the whole argument: the Bank's baseline had crude falling toward 75 dollars by mid-2027 from about 90 in Q2 2026, and WTI at 90.409 is on that path rather than above it. A downgrade to the energy-inflation risk is what starts pricing December.

catalysts.event: US: FOMC decision (October 27-28)
catalysts.note: A hold is priced at 75-80% with the hike at 20-25%, and the committee's own distribution argues for patience: 12 of 18 participants project a single 4.125% median for end-2026, one quarter-point move from the current 3.875% midpoint, which is a committee that has one hike left and no urgency about when. No projections at this meeting. Wednesday's core CPI at 0.3% or above is the only thing that makes it live.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB decision and press conference
catalysts.note: A hold is expected by 70 of 73 economists polled by Reuters on October 5-8 and priced at 88% by ECB Watch, with the deposit rate at 2.50%. The content is entirely in the press conference, because 64 of 73 of the same panel expect a quarter-point hike on December 17 when new projections arrive - the forward that just raised the euro to 0. Whether Lagarde protects that pricing against a bank sector minus 8.43% on the month is the question.

catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ decision and Quarterly Outlook Report (October 29-30)
catalysts.note: Priced as a hold by every source checked - prediction markets at 91-95% no change, futures-derived estimates at 17-26% for a hike, and TE's own forecast row at 1.25% - with no source above 26%. So the decision is not the event; the Outlook Report's inflation forecast revision is, and it is the whole tradeable item in the yen. Momma puts consecutive hikes at 20-30% and says a delay past January is extremely unlikely, and futures carry most of one hike by December.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA decision
catalysts.note: A hold is the base case after a unanimous September 29 hike to 4.60%, the highest in the G10, with Bullock having signalled less follow-up tightening than futures carried. TE's calendar shows no published forecast. Q3 CPI six days earlier is what decides it, and the RBNZ having decided on October 28 is the sequencing the AUD/NZD long is now paid for rather than a repricing.

catalysts.event: US midterm elections
catalysts.note: The date that gives the energy picture its political shape. Trump has pledged not to strike Iran before it, which has capped Brent through every escalation including this weekend's attack on Riyadh's airport; and the October 9 Russian diesel waiver, framed by Bloomberg as upending years of sanctions to tame fuel prices, runs to April 7, 2027 but was timed for this. Both the pledge and the political incentive expire here, which is the one reason USOIL is RANGE rather than SHORT.

catalysts.event: UK: Bank of England decision and Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.note: A quarter-point hike to 4.00% priced near 90% in money markets, up from 81% on October 9, with Oxford Economics at the same 90% and expecting February too while Berenberg expects one and doubts a cycle. The September split was 6-3 with Greene, Mann and Pill wanting the move, and Greene has voted to hike three meetings running. The Budget lands a week earlier and September CPI two weeks earlier; this is the meeting the restored GBP +1 score is built on, and December 17 is the following decision.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: general election
catalysts.note: Four days after the RBA and ten days after the RBNZ, and the only scheduled New Zealand risk that is not a data point. Relevant to the kiwi mainly as a reason not to carry a large position through the first week of November, with the currency near one-year lows and the curve already pricing 56.7bp of tightening by February.

catalysts.event: France: Assembly solemn vote on the whole 2027 budget
catalysts.note: The third and decisive scheduled vote, after the revenue half on October 20 and social security on October 27. If the text survives here the euro-area bank correction loses its sovereign driver; if it does not, the ordinance route still does not open until December 17 at midnight, so the gap between the two is where the OAT and the bank index would do their worst work.

catalysts.event: US: FOMC decision with projections (December 8-9)
catalysts.note: Priced in a 65-75% range across curves and the meeting the median dot points to: 4.1% for end-2026 against a current 3.875% midpoint is exactly one more quarter-point move, with 12 of 18 participants on that number. New projections land here too, and the row to watch is 2027, which the September table has at 4.1% as well - a hold through all of next year, not the cut this report had been carrying.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB policy assessment
catalysts.note: The next decision after five consecutive holds at 0%, with the October 22 minutes in between. September CPI at 1.0% from 0.8% with core at 0.5% sits inside the 0-2% band and gives no urgency, and Vice Chairman Martin hinted at lower-for-longer on October 8. The franc question is not the rate, it is whether an accelerated appreciation forces the intervention Rabobank has warned about.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB decision with new projections, and the French ordinance deadline
catalysts.note: Two things land on the same day. 64 of 73 economists polled by Reuters expect the quarter-point hike to 2.75% here, which is the forward that raised the euro to 0. And it is the date the French budget's 70-day debate period expires at midnight, which is the first point at which the government could legislate by ordinance. A hawkish ECB and an unresolved French budget arriving together is the tail risk in the euro that nothing between now and then prices.

catalysts.event: Escalation without supply loss: Hormuz, Saudi strikes and the Russian diesel waiver
catalysts.note: The weekend tested this and the answer was clear. The Houthis struck Riyadh's King Khalid airport again on Sunday after a Saturday attack Al Jazeera reports killed 12 and wounded 309 - the deadliest in the kingdom in over a decade, though a second Al Jazeera report gives three killed and 36 wounded across Riyadh and Abha, so the figures conflict - and claimed Aramco facilities were targeted too. Crude fell: WTI minus 1.57% to 90.409, Brent minus 1.28% to 103.377. Riyadh has restored pipeline flows to about 3.5 million bpd with France sending forces to protect Yanbu, and OFAC General License 135 of October 9 authorises Russian-origin diesel to April 7, 2027. Nearly 20 ships have been attacked near Hormuz in a month, with roughly 9.5 million bpd leaving the strait in the week to October 6, about 30% below prewar on Kpler's count. The market is no longer paying for escalation, which is what keeps USOIL RANGE and the CAD short clean.

catalysts.event: Gas is the energy inflation central banks are actually trading, and it has no political cap
catalysts.note: The cleanest asymmetry on the board this week. Crude and refined products are politically capped - a US-Russia diesel waiver, a pre-midterm pledge not to strike Iran, restored Saudi pipeline flows - while natural gas has no deal and no spare capacity. UK gas printed 204.00 GBp/thm, plus 11.12% on the week and plus 176.39% year to date; EU gas 81.53 EUR/MWh, plus 10.90% on the week and plus 189.52% year to date; German gas 79.27, plus 4.61% on the week and plus 164.21% year to date. EU storage is about 12 percentage points below last year with warnings it could end the winter under 30%. That is the content of Bailey's line that tolerance for energy-driven inflation is running out, the reason both GBP and EUR improve on an energy argument while USOIL stays RANGE, and the reason gas is a heavier headwind for GER40 than falling Brent is a tailwind.

catalysts.event: The euro-area bank correction and its sovereign driver
catalysts.note: The single cap on the euro upgrade. The Euro Stoxx Banks index is minus 8.43% on the month, entered a technical correction on October 8 and sits at its lowest since June, with Societe Generale, Credit Agricole and Deutsche Bank all more than 15% below recent highs. The drivers are a French-German spread that hit a decade high, sovereign debt at roughly 13% of bank assets at end-2025, and crowding after a three-year rally that tripled the sector since 2022. OAT-Bund has since compressed to 138.10bp from roughly 159bp, which is the mechanism by which this unwinds; Bloomberg reads the move as a reset rather than a crash, and one strategist expects pressure until yield curves and risk premia move sustainably lower. Banks are the heaviest EU50 sector, which is why that index is scored on this and not on the DAX.

geopolitics: The weekend ran the cleanest possible experiment on the oil risk premium and the answer was unambiguous: the conflict escalated sharply and the price went down. The Houthis struck Riyadh's King Khalid airport again on Sunday October 11, after a Saturday attack that Al Jazeera reports killed 12 people and wounded 309 and describes as the deadliest in the kingdom in over a decade - a second Al Jazeera report gives three killed and 36 wounded across Riyadh and Abha on the earlier strikes, so the casualty figures conflict across reports and that is stated rather than resolved - and they claimed Aramco oil facilities were targeted alongside the airport. This is a qualitative change: the war has moved from tankers in the Strait to mass-casualty strikes on the territory of the largest Gulf producer, and Saudi air defences are visibly being penetrated. Crude fell on it. WTI is 90.409, minus 1.57% on the day, plus 1.09% on the week and minus 10.83% on the month; Brent is 103.377, minus 1.28% on the day and plus 3.05% on the week. Two supply responses outran the escalation and both are new since yesterday's report. First, Riyadh has restored pipeline flows to about 3.5 million barrels a day after the East-West line was shut following the September 11 drone attack, with Yanbu on the Red Sea the remaining pressure point and France sending soldiers, radars and defence systems to protect the terminal. Second, and larger, on October 9 Trump announced a deal with Putin under which OFAC issued General License 135 authorising the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027. It covers US restrictions only - the EU and UK import bans and the 100-dollar product price cap remain in force - and the tonnages come from Trump's own post rather than a published bilateral document: more than 300,000 tonnes immediately, 500,000 in November, a million after that and up to three million more depending on refinery conditions. Russia permitted 500,000 tonnes of foreign diesel sales from October 10 after banning exports in July. US diesel futures fell 4% on Friday and European diesel futures tumbled as much as 8.3%; Zelensky condemned the deal and lawmakers from both US parties criticised it, and Bloomberg framed it as upending years of sanctions as the White House seeks ways to tame fuel prices before the midterms. The Hormuz picture underneath all this is unchanged at wartime intensity: nearly 20 commercial ships attacked near the Strait, the Gulf or off Oman in the past month, a tanker hit by a drone near Sohar over the weekend and another damaged by a projectile in the Strait per UKMTO, and roughly 9.5 million barrels a day leaving the Strait in the week to October 6, about 30% below prewar on Kpler's count. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to 90 dollars from 85 - below spot, which is itself a statement about where they think the premium goes. The FX reads follow, and three of them changed today. First and most important, the energy complex has split along political lines and that split is the trade of the week behind Wednesday's CPI. Crude and refined products are capped by policy: a diesel waiver, restored Saudi flows, and a pledge not to strike Iran before November 3. Natural gas has no deal, no spare capacity and European storage about 12 percentage points below last year, with warnings it could finish the winter under 30%. So gas rose double digits on the week while crude fell: UK gas 204.00 GBp/thm at plus 11.12% and plus 176.39% year to date, EU gas 81.53 EUR/MWh at plus 10.90% and plus 189.52%, German gas 79.27 at plus 4.61% and plus 164.21%. That is why sterling and the euro both improve on an energy-inflation argument this morning while USOIL stays RANGE - and why gas remains a heavier headwind for GER40 than falling Brent is a tailwind. Second, Canada. Yesterday's report used a Gulf of Mexico shut-in and a near-record-low SPR to argue for sizing the CAD short smaller; a weekend of mass-casualty strikes on Saudi Arabia produced a 1.5% fall in WTI instead, so the premium is being priced out rather than in. That matters because of the Bank's own arithmetic: Macklem said on September 21 that it can look through a temporary gasoline jump but not persistent higher energy costs and that oil near 100 dollars would push inflation up in the coming months, while the Bank's baseline assumed crude falling toward 75 by mid-2027 from about 90 in the second quarter of 2026. WTI at 90.409 is on that baseline, which removes the hawkish oil argument from the Canadian case entirely and makes the short cleaner, not weaker. Third, the US CPI consequence that almost nobody will price correctly. Wednesday's headline is expected at 3.6-3.7% on roughly 5% energy and 9% gasoline, and that measures September. The waiver suppressing those same prices was issued on October 9. So the print is a backward-looking read on an energy complex that executive action has since moved to reverse, three weeks before an election, and the committee is deciding on core at 0.2% m/m regardless. Treating a hot headline as hawkish on Wednesday is trading a month that policy has already begun to unwind. Fourth, the haven bid simply is not there. A mass-casualty attack on Saudi Arabia produced no gold rally - 4,192.26 is minus 0.04% on the day and minus 2.95% year to date - and no franc rally either, with EUR/CHF back above 0.93 at 0.93071 after three weekly declines and USD/CHF exactly flat on the week. Real yields near two-decade highs are setting the metals, which is why both XAU and XAG stay RANGE and why the week's only genuine binary for them is Wednesday's core print rather than anything in the Gulf.
